body.statement:
Fix \(d\geq1\), \(\alpha>0\), \(\beta>0\), \(\gamma>\beta\), and \(L\geq4\), and put \(S=\alpha+\beta\).  On \(\mathcal P(d,0,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\), for every \(n\geq2\), \(h\in(0,1]\), and every admissible projection rank \(k\geq1\), there is a total Borel estimator \(\widehat\tau^{(2)}_{n,h,k}(0)\), based only on \(O_{1:n}\), such that, with \(\ell=h k^{-1/d}\),
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P(d,0,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)}
 \mathbb E_P\left|\widehat\tau^{(2)}_{n,h,k}(0)-\tau_P(0)\right|
 \leq C\left\{h^\gamma+\ell^S+h^\gamma\ell^\alpha+
 \sqrt{\frac1{nh^d}\left(1+\frac{k}{nh^d}\right)}\right\}.
\]
Here admissible ranks form a fixed, geometrically spaced sequence, and every positive real target rank has an admissible rank within a constant factor.  Consequently the last display remains valid, after changing \(C\), for an arbitrary integer tuning target \(k\geq1\).  The estimator uses a one-sided local-polynomial equation, second-order projection corrections to both its matrix and vector moments, the exact Lebesgue projection Gram, singular-value flooring, and clipping; it consists only of sample moments and finite matrix operations.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(D=[0,1]^d\), \(D_h=hD\), and \(K_h(x)=h^{-d}{\bf1}_{D_h}(x)\).  All statements below are uniform over \(P\in\mathcal P(d,0,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\).  By \(\mathrm{def:exact\mbox{-}model}\), \(P_X\) is Lebesgue measure on the cube, the observations are i.i.d. by \(\mathrm{ass:iid\mbox{-}sampling}\), and
\[
 e(x)=g_P(x)/4\in[1/4,1/2],\qquad
 e\in\mathcal H_d^\alpha(L/4),\qquad
 \mu_0\in\mathcal H_d^\beta(L),\qquad
 \tau\in\mathcal H_d^\gamma(L).
 \tag{1}
\]
The first equality and interval use \(\mathrm{ass:local\mbox{-}propensity\mbox{-}shape}\), the definition \(r_0=1\), and \(\mathrm{ass:multiplier\mbox{-}envelope}\); the three smoothness assertions use the corresponding H\"older assumptions in \(\mathrm{def:exact\mbox{-}model}\).  The Bernoulli and interiority assumptions imply that every random scalar used below is uniformly bounded.

Let \(m_\gamma=\lceil\gamma\rceil-1\), and let \(v:D\to\mathbb R^{q_0}\) be a fixed Lebesgue-orthonormal basis for the polynomials of total degree at most \(m_\gamma\).  Thus \(q_0\) depends only on \((d,\gamma)\) and
\[
 \int_Dv(z)v(z)^{\mathsf T}\,dz=I_{q_0}.
 \tag{2}
\]
For a positive integer resolution \(q\), partition \(D\) into \(q^d\) half-open cubes and, on every cube, take all tensor polynomials of degree at least
\[
 p=m_\gamma+\max\{\lceil\alpha\rceil-1,\lceil\beta\rceil-1\}.
\]
Lebesgue orthonormalization gives a vector \(b_k:D\to\mathbb R^k\), where \(k=Mq^d\) and \(M\) is fixed by \((d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\), with the exact, nonrandom Gram
\[
 \Omega_k=\int_D b_k(z)b_k(z)^{\mathsf T}\,dz=I_k.
 \tag{3}
\]
These are the admissible ranks.  Their physical mesh is \(h/q=M^{1/d}h k^{-1/d}\), so writing \(\ell=h k^{-1/d}\) changes approximation bounds only by a fixed constant.  Taylor's formula on each mesh cube, using exactly the convention \(m=\lceil s\rceil-1\) in the definition of \(\mathcal H_d^s(L)\), gives the following facts.  If \(\Pi_k f=b_k^{\mathsf T}\int_D b_k f\) denotes the exact Lebesgue projection, then for every component \(v_a\),
\[
 \left\|(I-\Pi_k)\{v_a(e(h\,\cdot)-3/8)\}\right\|_2\leq C\ell^\alpha,
 \qquad
 \left\|(I-\Pi_k)\{\mu_0(h\,\cdot)-1/2\}\right\|_2\leq C\ell^\beta.
 \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, on each physical cube, multiply the order-\(\lceil\alpha\rceil-1\) Taylor polynomial of \(e\) by \(v_a\); it belongs to the displayed piecewise-polynomial space and its remainder is at most \(C\ell^\alpha\).  The second inequality is identical with \(\beta\).  Since orthogonal projection minimizes \(L_2(D)\) error, the cellwise bounds imply (4).  This also proves the required approximation property without adding a smoothness assumption on \(\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\).

Define the population local moments
\[
 Q=\int_Dv(z)e(hz)\{1-e(hz)\}v(z)^{\mathsf T}\,dz,
 \qquad
 R=\int_Dv(z)e(hz)\{1-e(hz)\}\tau(hz)\,dz,
 \tag{5}
\]
and put \(\theta=Q^{-1}R\) and \(\tau_h(hz)=v(z)^{\mathsf T}\theta\).  These are proof intermediates, not quantities supplied to the estimator.  Equations (1)--(2) give
\[
 \frac3{16}I_{q_0}\preceq Q\preceq\frac14I_{q_0}.
 \tag{6}
\]
Let \(p_\tau\) be the Taylor polynomial of \(\tau\) at zero of degree \(m_\gamma\).  The definition of the H\"older ball gives
\[
 \sup_{z\in D}|\tau(hz)-p_\tau(hz)|\leq Ch^\gamma.
\]
Because \(p_\tau(h\,\cdot)\) lies in the span of \(v\), subtracting its coefficient vector from \(Q^{-1}R\), using (6), and evaluating at \(z=0\) yields
\[
 |\tau_h(0)-\tau(0)|+\sup_{z\in D}|\tau_h(hz)-\tau(hz)|\leq Ch^\gamma.
 \tag{7}
\]
The same argument and \(|\tau|\leq3/4\) show \(\|\theta\|+\sup_D|v^{\mathsf T}\theta|\leq C\).

We now define the estimator explicitly.  Use the deterministic bounded pilots
\[
 \bar e=3/8,
 \qquad
 \bar\mu=1/2.
 \tag{8}
\]
For observation \(i\), let \(z_i=X_i/h\), \(K_i=K_h(X_i)\), \(v_i=v(z_i)\), and \(b_i=b_k(z_i){\bf1}_{D_h}(X_i)\).  Write \(\mathbb P_n f=n^{-1}\sum_i f(O_i)\) and \(\mathbb U_n H=\{n(n-1)\}^{-1}\sum_{i\ne j}H(O_i,O_j)\).  Set
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \widehat Q={}&\mathbb P_n\!left[K_i v_i A_i(A_i-\bar e)v_i^{\mathsf T}\right]\\
 &-\mathbb U_n\!\left[K_iK_jv_i(A_i-\bar e)b_i^{\mathsf T}\Omega_k^{-1}b_jA_jv_j^{\mathsf T}\right],\\
 \widehat R={}&\mathbb P_n\!\left[K_iv_i(Y_i-\bar\mu)(A_i-\bar e)\right]\\
 &-\mathbb U_n\!\left[K_iK_jv_i(A_i-\bar e)b_i^{\mathsf T}\Omega_k^{-1}b_j(Y_j-\bar\mu)\right].
\end{aligned}
 \tag{9}
\]
Thus both \(Q\) and \(R\) receive a localized second-order correction.  The cross-factor \(v_j^{\mathsf T}\) in the correction to \(Q\) is essential: after multiplication by \(\theta\), it produces the projection of \(e\tau_h\).

For a square matrix \(M\), define
\[
 \mathcal J_\lambda(M)=\{\mathfrak f_\lambda(M^{\mathsf T}M)\}^{-1}M^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad
 \mathfrak f_\lambda(V\operatorname{diag}(s_j^2)V^{\mathsf T})
 =V\operatorname{diag}(\max\{s_j^2,\lambda^2\})V^{\mathsf T},
 \tag{10}
\]
with \(\lambda=1/32\).  This is a continuous, everywhere-defined singular-value flooring map; it equals \(M^{-1}\) whenever the least singular value of \(M\) is at least \(\lambda\).  The announced estimator is
\[
 \widehat\tau^{(2)}_{n,h,k}(0)
 =\operatorname{clip}_{[-3/4,3/4]}
 \left\{v(0)^{\mathsf T}\mathcal J_\lambda(\widehat Q)\widehat R\right\}.
 \tag{11}
\]
Equations (2)--(3) are fixed polynomial integrals; (9)--(11) use finite sums and finite matrix operations.  Hence (11) is a total Borel, data-only map even if \(D_h\) contains no observations or \(\widehat Q\) is singular.

We next calculate its bias.  Put \(e^*(z)=e(hz)\), \(\mu_0^*(z)=\mu_0(hz)\), \(\tau^*(z)=\tau(hz)\), \(\Delta_e=e^*-\bar e\), and \(\Delta_0=\mu_0^*-\bar\mu\).  By the Bernoulli regression assumption and iterated expectation,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\widehat Q_1
 &=Q+\int_Dv\Delta_e e^*v^{\mathsf T},
 &\mathbb E\widehat Q_2
 &=-\int_Dv\Delta_e\Pi_k(e^*v^{\mathsf T}),\\
 \mathbb E\widehat R_1
 &=R+\int_Dv\Delta_e(\Delta_0+e^*\tau^*),
 &\mathbb E\widehat R_2
 &=-\int_Dv\Delta_e\Pi_k(\Delta_0+e^*\tau^*).
\end{aligned}
 \tag{12}
\]
For example, the first vector identity follows from
\[
 \mathbb E[(Y-\bar\mu)(A-\bar e)\mid X=x]
 =e(x)\{1-e(x)\}\tau(x)
 +\{e(x)-\bar e\}\{\mu_0(x)-\bar\mu+e(x)\tau(x)\},
\]
and the second-order identities follow from independence of the two observations and the exact Gram (3).  Let \(\widehat S=\widehat R-\widehat Q\theta\).  Since \(R-Q\theta=0\), subtraction in (12) gives, component by component,
\[
 \mathbb E\widehat S_a
 =\int_D v_a\Delta_e(I-\Pi_k)
 \{\Delta_0+e^*(\tau^*-\tau_h^*)\}.
\]
Self-adjointness and idempotence of the exact orthogonal projection turn this into
\[
 \mathbb E\widehat S_a
 =\left\langle(I-\Pi_k)(v_a\Delta_e),
 (I-\Pi_k)\{\Delta_0+e^*(\tau^*-\tau_h^*)\}\right\rangle_{L_2(D)}.
 \tag{13}
\]
By (4), (7), \(e^*\leq1/2\), and the contraction property of \(I-\Pi_k\),
\[
 \|\mathbb E\widehat S\|
 \leq C\ell^\alpha(\ell^\beta+h^\gamma)
 =C\{\ell^S+h^\gamma\ell^\alpha\}.
 \tag{14}
\]
This derives separately the nuisance-product term and the interaction between propensity approximation and contrast smoothing.

We also need stabilization, and do not assume it.  From (12),
\[
 B_Q:=\mathbb E\widehat Q-Q
 =\int_Dv\Delta_e(I-\Pi_k)(e^*v^{\mathsf T}).
\]
For unit vectors \(a,c\), projection orthogonality and (1)--(2) give
\[
 |a^{\mathsf T}B_Qc|
 \leq\|(a^{\mathsf T}v)\Delta_e\|_2
       \|e^*(c^{\mathsf T}v)\|_2
 \leq\frac18\cdot\frac12=\frac1{16}.
 \tag{15}
\]
Combining (6) and (15) yields
\[
 s_{\min}(\mathbb E\widehat Q)\geq1/8.
 \tag{16}
\]

It remains to derive the stochastic terms.  The first-order summands in both \(\widehat S\) and \(\widehat Q\) are bounded multiples of \(K_h(X)\), so uniform design gives
\[
 \mathbb E\|H_1(O)\|^2\leq C\int_{D_h}h^{-2d}\,dx=Ch^{-d}.
 \tag{17}
\]
For the second-order summands, orthonormality in (3) gives the exact Hilbert--Schmidt calculation
\[
 \int_D\!\int_D\{b_k(z_1)^{\mathsf T}b_k(z_2)\}^2,dz_1dz_2
 =\operatorname{tr}(\Omega_k^2)=k.
\]
After the two changes of variables \(x_j=hz_j\), this implies
\[
 \mathbb E\|H_2(O_1,O_2)\|^2\leq Ckh^{-2d}.
 \tag{18}
\]
The first conditional projection of \(H_2\) has squared norm at most \(Ch^{-d}\): conditional expectation integrates one copy of \(b_k\), and the resulting \(\Pi_k\)-term is bounded in \(L_2(D)\) by orthogonal-projection contraction; the remaining outer localization contributes \(h^{-d}\), exactly as in (17).  The same bound holds after interchanging the observations.

For completeness, symmetrize the possibly nonsymmetric kernel by replacing \(H_2(o_1,o_2)\) with \(\{H_2(o_1,o_2)+H_2(o_2,o_1)\}/2\), and incorporate \(H_1\) as \(\{H_1(o_1)+H_1(o_2)\}/2\).  The resulting unordered U-statistic is exactly the sum of the empirical and ordered-U terms in (9).  If \(H^\circ=H-\mathbb EH-H_1^\circ(o_1)-H_1^\circ(o_2)\), direct expansion shows that the three summands are pairwise orthogonal and therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(\mathbb U_nH)
 =\frac4n\mathbb E\|H_1^\circ(O)\|^2
 +\frac2{n(n-1)}\mathbb E\|H^\circ(O_1,O_2)\|^2.
\]
Using (17)--(18), and summing the fixed number of vector or matrix coordinates, proves
\[
 \mathbb E\|\widehat S-\mathbb E\widehat S\|^2
 +\mathbb E\|\widehat Q-\mathbb E\widehat Q\|_{\mathrm F}^2
 \leq C W_{n,h,k},
 \qquad
 W_{n,h,k}=\frac1{nh^d}+\frac{k}{n^2h^{2d}}.
 \tag{19}
\]
Thus \((nh^d)^{-1/2}\) is the nondegenerate empirical scale and \(\sqrt{k}/(nh^d)\) is the degenerate projection scale; neither has been suppressed.

Let \(\mathcal G=\{\|\widehat Q-\mathbb E\widehat Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1/16\}\).  Equations (16) and (19), Chebyshev's inequality when \(W_{n,h,k}\leq1\), and the trivial probability bound otherwise give
\[
 \mathbb P(\mathcal G^c)\leq C\min\{1,W_{n,h,k}\}
 \leq C\sqrt{W_{n,h,k}}.
 \tag{20}
\]
On \(\mathcal G\), the least singular value of \(\widehat Q\) exceeds \(1/16\), so the flooring in (10) is inactive and \(\|\widehat Q^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq16\).  Since clipping cannot increase distance from \(\tau(0)\in[-3/4,3/4]\), (7), (14), (19), and (20) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E|\widehat\tau^{(2)}_{n,h,k}(0)-\tau(0)|
 &\leq Ch^\gamma+C\mathbb E\{\|\widehat S\|{\bf1}_{\mathcal G}\}
      +\frac32\mathbb P(\mathcal G^c)\\
 &\leq C\left\{h^\gamma+\ell^S+h^\gamma\ell^\alpha
 +\sqrt{\frac1{nh^d}+\frac{k}{n^2h^{2d}}}\right\}\\
 &=C\left\{h^\gamma+\ell^S+h^\gamma\ell^\alpha
 +\sqrt{\frac1{nh^d}\left(1+\frac{k}{nh^d}\right)}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally, successive admissible dimensions have bounded ratio, so replacing an arbitrary target dimension by a nearest admissible one changes \(\ell\), \(k\), and the bound only by fixed constants.  This proves the claim for every \(n\geq2\), including the cases in which a variance term exceeds one.
